name: אָמוֹן
summary: Above all Amon son of Manasseh, king of Judah for two years, who did evil as his father had and did not humble himself, and was killed by his servants; his son Josiah reigned after him (2Ki 21:18–26; 2Ch 33:20–25), and he is in the genealogy of Jesus (Mat 1:10). Also Amon the governor of Samaria, to whom Ahab sent Micaiah (1Ki 22:26; 2Ch 18:25), and the head of a family of Solomon's servants among the returned exiles (Neh 7:59), called Ami in Ezr 2:57. The spelling is the word of Pro 8:30, אָמוֹן “master workman” (or one brought up); it may also be read as “faithful”, from the root. The Egyptian god Amun (Jer 46:25; Nah 3:8), spelled alike, is another word, borrowed from Egyptian.

evidence.note: “And אָמוֹן his son reigned in his place.”
“The servants of Amon conspired against him and killed the king in his house.”
“He did not humble himself before Yahweh as Manasseh his father had humbled himself.”
“Manasseh begot Amon, and Amon begot Josiah.”
“Take Micaiah and bring him back to אָמֹן the governor of the city.”
Among the sons of Solomon's servants: “the sons of אָמוֹן”.
The same family, “the sons of Ami (אָמִי)”.
“Then I was beside him אָמוֹן”: the common noun spelled as the name.

note: Takes a.dy.ao (20 tokens counted, shared with a.dy.an by spelling). Its count includes Jer 46:25 and Nah 3:8, the god Amun of No (Thebes), which is not this name: the TIPNR record Amon@Jer.46.25 (Supernatural) is not named in people. Jer 52:15 הָאָמוֹן is הֶהָמוֹן “the multitude” (2Ki 25:11). Whether the name means “workman”, “nursling” or “faithful” is read from the form; scripture does not explain it.
